Save perhaps one. It is the idea, fantastical to many as it is irresistible to others, that the Democrats will win a statewide race in Texas for the first time in 32 years. According to the latest New York Times/Siena University poll of the race for U.S. Senate, James Talarico, a 37-year-old state legislator seen by national Democrats as one of the breakout stars of this cycle, is ahead of his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, the state’s scandal-plagued attorney general, by six points. The poll was conducted from Sept. 21 to Sept. 30. A survey from mid-September, the ReconMR/Siena Research Institute poll, also showed the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Gina Hinojosa, four points ahead of the three-term G.O.P. incumbent, Greg Abbott, the most dominant political figure in Texas. Cue the fluttering heartbeats. Cue, as well, the eye-rolls. Given how thoroughly Republicans have dominated the state, and how the hopes of Democrats have repeatedly crashed, some Texas pollsters remain skeptical. “At some point, you do get conditioned by all that’s happened in the past,” said James Henson, the director of the University of Texas at Austin’s Texas Politics Project. “I mean, you look at the trends and you have to admit that something’s going on. But you still don’t want to believe your lying eyes, because you’ve been burned for so long.” Mr. Henson was referring to the perennial spectacle of much-ballyhooed Texas Democratic aspirants face-planting against the Lone Star State’s red wall. First came Tony Sanchez Jr., the swaggering and self-funding Laredo oilman whom Gov. Rick Perry dispatched in 2002 by an 18-point margin. Next was the state senator Wendy Davis, who attracted worldwide attention for her filibuster in the Texas Legislature against an anti-abortion measure but whom Mr. Abbott demolished by 20 points in 2014. Finally, the El Paso congressman Beto O’Rourke came up 2.6 points short of defeating Senator Ted Cruz in 2018 but then suffered a 10-point loss to Mr. Abbott four years later. Even with the awareness of such humiliations, Democrats find themselves maintaining that 2026 could, at long last, be the year. President Trump’s deep unpopularity and the prospect of a blue wave could, they insist, extend into the state he won by nearly 14 points in 2024. According to a September survey conducted by Texas Southern University, Mr. Trump is seven points underwater in Texas. Mr. Talarico has run an energetic and well-financed campaign, while Mr. Paxton has staged far fewer public events and has had to rely on outside groups to fund an attack-ad blitzkrieg against his Democratic opponent. Mr. Abbott, meanwhile, has outspent Ms. Hinojosa by a 10-to-one ratio, yet has been unable to build an insurmountable lead. “People have vastly underestimated Gina,” said Ms. Davis, now a political consultant and a senior adviser to Planned Parenthood Texas Votes, an advocacy organization. “Dollar for dollar, she’s running the best statewide campaign we’ve ever seen.” Such optimism stands in defiance of the political axiom that Texas is where idealistic Democrats go to be mugged by reality. The party’s demise there is not a product of ill fortune, Mr. Henson said. “Governor Abbott has built an impressive election machine that has benefited state-level Republicans again and again for a decade and a half,” he said. “And the Democratic machinery here is almost nonexistent.” A ‘Hollowing-Out’ I have written about the politics of my native state at regular intervals for more than three decades. After watching the Democrats’ century-long rule in Texas come to a decisive end with Gov. Ann Richards’s loss to George W. Bush in 1994, I saw the party descend into atrophy in which failure begot more failure. “The 30-year drought has done a lot of things,” said Luke Warford, the chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party and the founder of the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund. “It’s kept donors on the sidelines, which makes a lot of potentially good candidates not run because there’s no belief they can win. And it also makes a lot of really talented staff leave to find better-paying work in true battleground states.” The Democratic Party has no counterpart to Mr. Abbott, and hasn’t since 1993, when Senator Lloyd Bentsen moved to Washington to join President Bill Clinton’s cabinet. Its weaknesses are even more glaring farther down the hierarchy. In recent elections, as many as one-third of state races have gone uncontested by Democrats. One-fifth of the party’s county chairs and two-thirds of its precinct chairs have been left unfilled. Until last year, the state party had a negative operating budget. As the veteran Democratic consultant Matt Angle observed, “There’s been a hollowing-out of the party.” Still, those of us who recall the satisfied sense of invincibility among Texas Democrats after roughly a century of one-party rule have detected similar signs of overconfidence among the state’s ruling party. The party’s rightward tilt, increasingly forceful with each legislative session, reached its apotheosis in March, with Mr. Paxton’s primary victory over the more moderate Republican four-term incumbent, Senator John Cornyn. Mr. Paxton, a close ally of Mr. Trump’s, was impeached by the Republican-controlled State House (and later acquitted by the State Senate) in 2023 over allegations that included bribery. He was also accused by his wife of adultery. Mr. Trump endorsed him anyway, all but guaranteeing his landslide primary triumph over Mr. Cornyn but in the process testing the allegiance of center-right Texans. In similar fashion, the Texas G.O.P. is in danger of losing many Latino voters who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 after years of siding with Democrats. “We adopted a lazy way of campaigning that bit us on the ass, and we’ve learned from that,” Mr. O’Rourke said. “Now it’s the Republicans who’ve gotten really lazy and complacent and comfortable.” Signs of Republican Overreach Simply spending one week driving through the vastness of Texas, as I did in September, is all it takes to appreciate an underdog party’s uphill battle. The state’s 32 million residents are spread across 20 media markets, many of them distinct ecosystems, from the urban colossi of Houston and the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex to the oil patch of the Texas Panhandle to the Latino-dominated borderlands of the Rio Grande Valley. “When national donors are deciding where to invest, they look at a place like Iowa, where $5 million can fully fund a race,” said Katherine Fischer, the director of the Texas Majority PAC, which was established by the liberal philanthropist Soros family. “That’s why Texas is always at the bottom of their list. It’s just so damned big.” Reaching so many markets presents a daunting challenge for an upstart candidate like Ms. Hinojosa, a state representative from the border city of Brownsville. “There’s still 20 percent of the electorate that doesn’t know who I am,” she said in an interview in mid-September. To date, Ms. Hinojosa’s campaign has said that it has raised about $20 million. For his part, Mr. Talarico spent about $30 million earlier this year to introduce himself statewide as a man of Christian faith and a member of the Texas House with a record of supporting bipartisan legislation. Since that time, however, Mr. Paxton and his associates have invested more than $100 million in an effort to redefine his opponent as “radical” and “weird,” with ads that quote from remarks Mr. Talarico made several years ago (and later renounced) suggesting that “God is nonbinary” and that there are six biological sexes. Mr. Paxton and his allies have at times questioned Mr. Talarico’s manhood and even his Christianity, an effort to jolt the sensibilities of a state prone to mythologizing godly and masculine archetypes. “How they’re negatively defining Talarico is kind of a bank-shot way of saying that he’s not a true Texas conservative,” Mr. Henson said. Whether money can overwhelm conditions on the ground is the riddle looming over the Texas races. In the border city of Laredo, which Mr. Trump won in 2024 — the first time a Republican had done so in over a century — signs of buyer’s remorse are evident. Arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Laredo were higher in July than in any other American city. Mr. Trump’s erratic trade policies have further created instability at the city’s port of entry. While acknowledging the economic concerns that many border residents share, Adrian Zapata, a business executive in the health industry who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said in an interview that the negative ads against Mr. Talarico were resonating with some of his family members. “They see Talarico as an ultraliberal,” he said. “They’re done with the ‘they/them.’ They’re going to vote for Paxton just because of that.” As for Mr. Zapata, “I’m not ready to vote for Talarico,” he said. “But I don’t like Paxton. He’s never done anything for South Texas, and his personal and business dealings have hurt him a lot with folks down here.” There is a similarly muddled electoral picture in the cattle country of deep West Texas adjacent to Big Bend National Park. Mr. Trump and Mr. Abbott have aggressively championed a border wall and artificial intelligence data centers, both of which threaten to disrupt the region’s pastoral ethos. A coalition of more than 200 landowners has sued the federal government over the border wall, while other residents have circulated a petition to protest the construction of a new data center near Fort Stockton. George Johnson, a cattle feed operator in Alpine, waved off such concerns, saying: “Folks worrying about data centers were also worried when the internet got started. It’s Talarico who scares me to death, him and all that socialist talk.” Others in this largely conservative region harbor the view that Republicans have failed to make good on their promises. Thaddeus Cleveland, the Republican sheriff of Terrell County, said that both he and his county had voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, but added, “Everything he campaigned on, we’re seeing the opposite of, like going to war.” Sheriff Cleveland predicted that the negative campaign ads by the Republicans would not factor as significantly into the votes of his neighbors as “the price of groceries and gas, which are compounded here because we’re so far from everywhere else.” But it is in purple Tarrant County, dominated by Fort Worth, where the party could pay the price for having potentially overestimated its mandate from the voters. Conservative leaders have cut funds for nonprofits that aid at-risk children, subjected school library books to right-wing litmus tests and eliminated free bus rides to polling stations in poor neighborhoods. “The far-right leaders here have implemented Project 2025 on a county level,” said Alisa Simmons, a Democrat and county commissioner who is running to unseat the conservative county judge, Tim O’Hare. In an early sign this year that area Republicans may be out of step with Tarrant County’s constituents, a Democratic aviation machinist and union leader, Taylor Rehmet, defeated Leigh Wambsganss, a well-funded Republican Christian activist who led the conservative takeover of several metroplex school boards. He won by 14 points in a January special election for a State Senate seat covering a region that Mr. Trump won by 17 points in 2024. A ‘Gradualist’ Theory Which party prevails in Texas is a complicated riddle. Historically a low-turnout state — it ranked second to last in the 2024 election, ahead of only Arkansas — Texas held a primary in March that saw nearly one in four voters showing up to the polls, a modern record for midterm participation, with Democrats slightly outpacing Republicans. A few factors could conspire to thwart a blue wave in Texas. As of 2020, straight-ticket voting is no longer possible in the state, which could impact the mostly Democratic urban counties where that practice has frequently been used by voters in past elections. Texas is one of only eight states that lack universal online registration, while voting by mail is also highly restricted. In January, Mr. Abbott turned over the state’s list of approximately 18.7 million registered voters to the Trump administration, and 1.2 million of them have subsequently been put on the “suspense list” because their addresses have not been verified. The recent shuttering of nearly one-third of Tarrant County’s polling sites by its Republican-controlled county commission is particularly worrisome for Democrats. “The reason we’ve lost these statewide races in the past is because we’ve never gotten enough out of Tarrant County to overcome the margins in rural Texas,” Ms. Davis said of the turnout. “If we don’t get it to 53 or 54 percent this November, it’s game over. James and Gina can’t win.” But the state’s Republicans have reasons of their own to be fretful. Partly because of the recruitment efforts of the Texas Majority PAC and Blueprint Texas, a down-ballot candidate support organization co-founded by Ms. Davis earlier this year, the Democrats are fielding a full slate in all 150 state races for the first time in a half-century. Though many of these aspirants face long odds, their presence on the ballot could energize the Democrats in predominantly conservative regions who have not bothered to turn out in the past. “If we win on Nov. 3, most of those names running down-ballot in really tough areas like East Texas and the Hill Country and the Panhandle will be responsible,” Mr. O’Rourke said. Mr. Henson added that while he remained skeptical about Democratic enthusiasm being sufficient to carry the day for Mr. Talarico, he also doubted that a last-minute avalanche of negative ads would prove decisive for Mr. Paxton. “At a certain point, there’s diminishing impact once you get past an absurd level of spending,” he said. Rather than project a winner in November, Mr. Henson said he felt more comfortable embracing a “gradualist” theory, one in which Texas does not become blue overnight, but instead competitive. “Even if Talarico loses by a Beto-like margin,” he said, “the next cycle is a presidential election, where Trump likely won’t be popular and Democratic turnout will be higher. body:
I'm endorsing three more Democrats for Congress. Let's help them finish strong in the final seven days.
#
We've got just one week until Election Day, Peter, and I've got three more candidates I'd like you to meet.
[](https://act.timwalz.com/go/73?c0=stp-ms-em-20261027-1.JXSOkA&amount=5&refcode=em20261027-1265&t=1&akid=1265%2E34582%2E4Cui5L)
Today, I'm proud to endorse three more Democrats running for Congress in critical races across the country: Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania, Denise Powell in Nebraska, and Mitch Berman in Wisconsin.
**[With just seven days until Election Day, these candidates need our help to finish strong. If you're ready to join me in supporting them, chip in $5 or whatever works for you to Small Town PAC today →](https://act.timwalz.com/go/73?c0=stp-ms-em-20261027-1.JXSOkA&amount=5&refcode=em20261027-1265&t=2&akid=1265%2E34582%2E4Cui5L)**
I launched Small Town PAC back in April to put power back in the hands of our neighbors and help Democrats compete in places too many people have written off.
That means supporting teachers, nurses, veterans, labor leaders, and other working people who understand their communities because they've spent their lives serving them.
And these three candidates are exactly the kind of people I had in mind:
**Bob Brooks (PA-07)** is a firefighter and union leader who spent more than 20 years serving his community in eastern Pennsylvania. Now, he's running to bring that same commitment to working people to Congress.
**Denise Powell (NE-02)** is a mom, small business owner, and community leader who's spent years fighting to protect public schools and helping more Nebraskans run for office.
**Mitch Berman (WI-01)** grew up in a working-class family in rural Wisconsin and became an emergency room nurse. He's spent more than a decade caring for veterans and their families, and now he's running to take that experience to Washington.
These are folks who know what working families are up against. They've spent their careers looking out for their neighbors, and they're ready to do the same in Congress.
_But here's the deal: Endorsements alone don't win elections._
Our candidates are up against Republican opponents and wealthy special interests who would love nothing more than to keep working people out of power. And with just one week left, they need every resource they can get to reach voters and finish strong.
**[Peter, will you chip in $5 or whatever you can today to help Small Town PAC support Bob, Denise, Mitch, and our entire slate of endorsed candidates in these final seven days?](https://act.timwalz.com/go/73?c0=stp-ms-em-20261027-1.JXSOkA&amount=5&refcode=em20261027-1265&t=3&akid=1265%2E34582%2E4Cui5L)**
**[Donate $5 ››](https://act.timwalz.com/go/73?c0=stp-ms-em-20261027-1.JXSOkA&amount=5&refcode=20261027-1265&t=22&akid=1265%2E34582%2E4Cui5L)**
We've got good people running. Now let's help them get across the finish line.
With gratitude,
Tim

| | "I'm so glad I live in a world where there are Octobers." As Anne of Green Gables reminds us, fall is a wonderful season to slow down, savor the little things, and make lasting family memories. With crisp air, colorful leaves, pumpkin spice favorites, and the excitement of a new season, there are countless ways to enjoy this special time of year together. From decorating your home with pumpkins and fall crafts to creating a family gratitude tree, visiting a pumpkin patch or corn maze, and whipping up delicious seasonal treats, you don't have to plan an elaborate outing to make the season memorable. Cozy movie nights, family getaways, campfires, and simple evenings spent laughing together can become some of your children's favorite memories. And don't forget one important fall tradition! Grab a pumpkin spice latte and make your voice heard at the ballot box. Election season is also a wonderful opportunity to talk with your children about American freedom, responsible citizenship, and the importance of participating in our nation's future. Whether you're embracing fall with festive activities, meaningful family traditions, or a little patriotic spirit, we've gathered seven ideas to help you make the most of this beautiful season. | | | Peter, I always knew we could win this race. But when we began, I would not have dared to believe that our coalition would build and expand so quickly. I have been inspired by the coming together of farmers and veterans, nurses and doctors, parents and students, Democrats, Republicans, and Independents. You made that happen. You willed this movement into existence with your dollars, your volunteering, and your faith (along with some constructively-channeled righteous anger). **You evened the odds in the race that could well decide the fate of Congress and the country.** _Take a second to appreciate what you have helped us pull off..._ → Our poll numbers show we’re in a dead heat with John McGuire in a district he won by 15 points, just two years ago. Better yet, when voters hear a comparison of McGuire’s voting history and what I have done for our region, I start pulling away with the lead. → The DCCC elevated us to their Red to Blue target list, making it official: the path back to sanity runs through VA-05. → McGuire is running defense. He’s refused public debates, refused to explain his stock trades, and refused to explain why he cast the sole vote against a Virginia bill to end child marriage.

→ We’re barnstorming through all 21 counties and 3 municipalities of this district every single week. Our amazing grassroots team is knocking thousands of doors. → We launched our final ad, and are working overtime to keep it on the air so we can reach as many undecided and sporadic voters as possible before Election Day. Now we are 7 days out. This is the final window to talk to voters before November 3rd – every second counts. **My team and I set a goal of raising another $50K online by October 31st to fund our final GOTV push. We are counting down the campaign now in days – soon to be by hours! – and every penny right now goes to voter contact. Donations between now and Saturday will determine how many undecided voters we can turn out Sunday through Tuesday.** **[If you can give any amount toward our $50K online goal before we close out October, it will impact what we can get done on the ground. body:
Because this isn't easy. It's an absolute dogfight, and you have to love the fight, really love it, to keep pushing when the odds are stacked against you.

| Please don't take my appreciation for granted, Friend.The love I have for you, for Minnesota, and for this country. How many people can say they've put everything on the line and have been within striking distance of making history by flipping Minnesota - a Democrat stronghold - to the Republican column?Not many. Because this isn't easy. It's an absolute dogfight, and you have to love the fight, really love it, to keep pushing when the odds are stacked against you.That's exactly what I've done. And I'm not backing down now.I've dedicated everything I have to flipping the US Senate seat in Minnesota, and there is no question in my mind that this is the right choice when I've seen first-hand what Peggy Flanagan and Tim Walz have done. A Marine. A grieving dad. A promise to keep.
Peter,

I want to tell you why I'm running, and I want to do it straight.

My son was a United States Marine. He followed me into the Corps, and he came home proud of his service. Then one night, in our own hometown, he was murdered. For a long time after that, nothing happened. No leads, no arrests, no answers — just a quiet phone and a family trying to put one foot in front of the other. I do not have the words for what that kind of waiting does to a father.

But I learned one thing in those years. Sitting still was not going to bring my son back, and it was not going to keep another family from getting the knock on the door that I got. So I made him a promise. No other dad would bury his child the way I buried mine. Not if I could help it.

I ran for Hemet City Council on that promise, and I won. Every day since, I have gone to work on public safety — better policing, cleaner streets, real consequences for the people who hurt our families. We have made real progress. But the truth is, a city can only do so much when Washington is asleep at the wheel.

**That is why I'm running for Congress.**

Crime is up. Our borders are open. Career politicians in D.C. cash their checks and look the other way. They don't see what we see. They don't lose what families like mine have lost. I do, and I am not going to stop fighting until that changes.

| | **In Case You Missed It**
**Janoo’s Solution for Housing is to “Limit Residents and Businesses”**
A recent WPTZ report summarized Janoo’s “post-growth” plan to address housing costs in Vermont the following way:
**“To address Vermont’s housing crisis,_Janoo says she wants to limit the number _****_of residents and businesses moving to the state._****”**
* Source: NBC5, WPTZ, _Who is Amanda Janoo, the Democratic Candidate for Vermont governor_ , Cusanelli and Maloney, Monday, October 26, 2026

**Now, compare Janoo’s position to Governor Phil Scott’s** : “As I say all the time, **we need more taxpayers, not more taxes** ...we know mortgages and rents are unaffordable for many. Housing costs drive people out of Vermont and prevent families, workers, and good jobs from moving here. **To me, the issue is obvious.** ”
\-- Governor Phil Scott To paraphrase Forest Gump ... that’s all we have to say about that.

Peter,I’ll be honest: I got a little emotional writing this.

**In just the first two weeks of October, this campaign raised $99,847 from more than 200 individual donors. Almost all of them live right here in Wisconsin.**

Last Thursday night, around 8:00 p.m., Gina, our campaign manager, filed our latest FEC report. She filed it from a bar in Wausau, laptop open, with a big smile on her face (you can see the photo below).

That isn’t PAC money or a few big checks from out of state. It’s people from across Wisconsin who decided this race matters enough to chip in what they could. I’m blown away by every one of them.

Over the same two weeks, Michael Alfonso raised just over $2,000 from 10 individual donors, and only three of them live within 500 miles of Wisconsin. He also took $19,000 from PACs, including $5,000 from AIPAC.

It shows who each of us will answer to. Michael will answer to the rich and to corporations. I’ll answer to my constituents.

We have one week left. What we raise now keeps our TV ad on the air through Election Day and keeps our message in front of voters who are still making up their minds.

Peter,I’ll be honest: I got a little emotional writing this.

**In just the first two weeks of October, this campaign raised $99,847 from more than 200 individual donors. Almost all of them live right here in Wisconsin.**

Last Thursday night, around 8:00 p.m., Gina, our campaign manager, filed our latest FEC report. She filed it from a bar in Wausau, laptop open, with a big smile on her face (you can see the photo below).

That isn’t PAC money or a few big checks from out of state. It’s people from across Wisconsin who decided this race matters enough to chip in what they could. I’m blown away by every one of them.

Over the same two weeks, Michael Alfonso raised just over $2,000 from 10 individual donors, and only three of them live within 500 miles of Wisconsin. He also took $19,000 from PACs, including $5,000 from AIPAC.

It shows who each of us will answer to. Michael will answer to the rich and to corporations. I’ll answer to my constituents.

We have one week left. What we raise now keeps our TV ad on the air through Election Day and keeps our message in front of voters who are still making up their minds.

clean_body: Hundreds of you stepped up| | | Peter,I’ll be honest: I got a little emotional writing this. In just the first two weeks of October, this campaign raised $99,847 from more than 200 individual donors. Almost all of them live right here in Wisconsin. Last Thursday night, around 8:00 p.m., Gina, our campaign manager, filed our latest FEC report. She filed it from a bar in Wausau, laptop open, with a big smile on her face (you can see the photo below). That isn’t PAC money or a few big checks from out of state. It’s people from across Wisconsin who decided this race matters enough to chip in what they could. I’m blown away by every one of them. Over the same two weeks, Michael Alfonso raised just over $2,000 from 10 individual donors, and only three of them live within 500 miles of Wisconsin. He also took $19,000 from PACs, including $5,000 from AIPAC. It shows who each of us will answer to. Michael will answer to the rich and to corporations. I’ll answer to my constituents. Hi everyone. This is Kelly Morrison. We’re one week out from Election Day, and our voter turnout push is in full swing. But even though it’s firing on all cylinders, it’s not fully funded – **there’s more we can do**. I know this team always steps up when it matters most, so I sat down to write this email asking for your support. But then my husband John jumped in and informed me that he is a very effective fundraiser for my campaign. In fact, he suggested that if _he_ asked you, we might even raise more. I clearly can’t just take his word for it, so we decided to put it to the test. We’re both sharing messages with you in this email, and we’ll each ask you to donate – whoever raises more will have bragging rights for all time, and of course, every penny will go directly toward the critical work left to win the midterms.I get to go first and I’ve already taken up some of your time, so I’m making my ask very short and to the point: This midterm election is one of the most consequential of our lifetime. What happens one week from today will determine the damage Trump can do over the next two years – and with the possibility of a Supreme Court vacancy, it will also determine the damage his legacy can do over the next several decades or even generations. [**We cannot afford not to put every ounce of effort into this, so I’m humbly asking you:****will you contribute $25 to our Get Out the Vote budget to fully fund this push and make sure we can turn out every possible voter in MN-03?**](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/142288976/656431825/-1066768109?amount=25&refcode=261027em_kmjw_kelly&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNTkvMS8xMDkzOTAiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiOTIwNzU4NmYtMWJkMi1mMTExLWJmNWItMDAwZDNhNGZiZDUwIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=4Gn8fG58rOFKFzE0W8WlIYOr14eJMainaMTawTi7-S4=)

Hi everyone! John Willoughby here. I think it’s an unfair advantage that Kelly’s message got top billing – but she is the Congresswoman here, after all.Here’s my pitch to you: I’d like to think I know better than anyone how hard Kelly works for the people of Minnesota and how much she cares for every single person across the district and entire state. I’ve been lucky to get a front-row seat to her incredible work in the state legislature and in Congress. But I’m certainly not the only one who knows all that – everyone who has ever met or talked with Kelly could say the exact same thing. _Because the truth is, Kelly treats every constituent like a member of her own family. _ **She fights just as hard for you as she would for herself, or for our kids, or for me – because that’s just who she is.** I’m willing to bet you agree that Congress is in _desperate_ need of that kind of compassionate, effective leader right now. There are way too many corrupt, self-serving, power-hungry politicians walking the halls of the Capitol. And if Kelly’s opponent were to flip this seat, there’d be one more. That’s the last thing Minnesotans want or need. But the GOP is going to try. Trump has already waded into our state’s elections, and his super PAC “MAGA, Inc.” is spending millions of dollars here to turn out Republican voters. We can’t leave anything to chance – we’d just never forgive ourselves. Friend, Early on in the campaign, w _hen reporters finally caught up with Marsha Blackburn_ to ask her why she refusesd to step onto a debate stage or even answer unscripted questions from voters and journalists, her answer was _ **"I'm talking to Tennesseans every day."**_ _****_**_Really?_** Because it’s been nearly _**a decade since she held an open, public in-person town hall**_. Instead of answering to everyday Tennesseans, she hides behind invite-only corporate fundraisers, tightly scripted media appearances, and pre-screened phone calls where no one can challenge her record. When she says she’s talking to Tennesseans, she means high-dollar donors and political insiders. **Well, I actually talk to everyday Tennesseans every single day— _and here is what they are telling me:_**
* **They are suffocating under everyday costs.** They want real relief—like eliminating the state grocery tax, capping prescription drug costs, and lowering monthly energy bills—not more tax giveaways for out-of-state corporations.
* **They are furious about state politicians starving our public schools.** Parents and teachers across all 95 counties are tired of voucher schemes that strip millions out of neighborhood classrooms to subsidize private school tuition for wealthy families.
* **They want healthcare they can actually rely on. **They’re tired of local hospital closures and healthcare monopolies like Ballad Health driving up medical prices while cutting patient services. They want us to expand Medicaid and break up healthcare cartels.
* **They are sick of corruption, corporate graft, and backroom deals. **They want leaders who answer to working people—not out-of-state nuclear waste companies or pharmaceutical lobbies.

_**Marsha Blackburn can dodge debates, skip town halls, and ignore the public, but she cannot avoid the voters on Election Day.**_ Tennessee doesn’t need another career politician who treats voters like a photo op. We need a Governor who stands with working families, listens to local communities, and shows up to fight for them every single day. clean_body: | Friend, Early on in the campaign, w hen reporters finally caught up with Marsha Blackburn to ask her why she refusesd to step onto a debate stage or even answer unscripted questions from voters and journalists, her answer was "I'm talking to Tennesseans every day." **Really? Because it’s been nearly a decade since she held an open, public in-person town hall. Instead of answering to everyday Tennesseans, she hides behind invite-only corporate fundraisers, tightly scripted media appearances, and pre-screened phone calls where no one can challenge her record. When she says she’s talking to Tennesseans, she means high-dollar donors and political insiders. Well, I actually talk to everyday Tennesseans every single day— and here is what they are telling me: They are suffocating under everyday costs. They want real relief—like eliminating the state grocery tax, capping prescription drug costs, and lowering monthly energy bills—not more tax giveaways for out-of-state corporations. They are furious about state politicians starving our public schools. Parents and teachers across all 95 counties are tired of voucher schemes that strip millions out of neighborhood classrooms to subsidize private school tuition for wealthy families. They want healthcare they can actually rely on. They’re tired of local hospital closures and healthcare monopolies like Ballad Health driving up medical prices while cutting patient services. They want us to expand Medicaid and break up healthcare cartels. They are sick of corruption, corporate graft, and backroom deals. They want leaders who answer to working people—not out-of-state nuclear waste companies or pharmaceutical lobbies. Marsha Blackburn can dodge debates, skip town halls, and ignore the public, but she cannot avoid the voters on Election Day. Tennessee doesn’t need another career politician who treats voters like a photo op. We need a Governor who stands with working families, listens to local communities, and shows up to fight for them every single day. Can you believe it's election season again? Election Day is next Tuesday, November 3, and early voting is already underway in many states. With just one week to go, the political landscape looks very different from the one that brought Republicans back to power.
President Trump's approval rating has fallen to[ 33 percent](https://substack.com/redirect/22292f0a-3b9b-4119-9286-581b738b372b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) as his war with Iran has grown[ increasingly unpopular](https://substack.com/redirect/8f4b5e92-4a98-48ec-8b3b-9508b548bc7c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Meanwhile, rising gas prices and stubborn inflation are hitting American families and small businesses at home, and some of the voters who helped put Republicans in power are beginning to look for something different.
The parallels with the 2006 midterms are hard to miss. By the fall of that year, George W. Bush's approval rating had fallen to about[ 38 percent](https://substack.com/redirect/5039737c-4cb7-4539-ae9f-cffb38dd7b35?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) as an unpopular Iraq War and growing economic anxiety weighed on Republicans. Democrats went on to gain[ 31 House seats](https://substack.com/redirect/55e70a08-55b6-4bf5-a7e8-b5d0ce5100aa?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), winning control of the chamber for the[ first time in 12 years](https://substack.com/redirect/89241267-6544-4973-a2ef-7e231006895a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and breaking through in districts that had long seemed out of reach.
I was one of the unlikely candidates who helped make that happen. At 31, fresh from Iraq, I ran in a[ Republican-leaning](https://substack.com/redirect/957156d8-6512-43fb-a25a-942f86a3364b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) Bucks County, Pa., district that Bush had carried two years earlier. Washington saw me as a long shot.
We proved them wrong.
We won by[ 1,521 votes](https://substack.com/redirect/6e8119a0-9dc7-4b23-ae6d-633914bdee80?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) -- 50.3 percent to 49.7 percent -- becoming the first Iraq War veteran elected to Congress and flipping a Republican-held seat in one of the defining upset victories of that election. It was a historic win in a historic election, and it gave me a firsthand understanding of what happens when the political ground suddenly shifts beneath a party's feet. More importantly, it taught me a lesson Democrats should remember now: a favorable political climate can create an opening, but it cannot build a majority on its own. Winning still requires persuading voters who did not start out on the Democratic side and then leading them to a better America.
The shift is showing up on the map. The[ Cook Political Report](https://substack.com/redirect/89bad158-091f-4ced-b3e7-1dbcf0a97def?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) recently moved Texas and Iowa from "Lean Republican" to "Toss Up," expanding the core Senate battlefield from four states to six. The Senate itself, once widely viewed as out of reach for Democrats, is now[ increasingly competitive](https://substack.com/redirect/bc3b2cd8-6a4f-4075-a6bf-8d2ca76e984f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). But a favorable map is not a coalition. Democrats still have to persuade the voters who are making those races competitive.
The discontent extends beyond Democrats.[ Seventy-one percent](https://substack.com/redirect/22292f0a-3b9b-4119-9286-581b738b372b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of Americans disapprove of President Trump's handling of the cost of living, including four in 10 Republicans. Among[ independents](https://substack.com/redirect/7429d069-8f41-4564-a85e-8e816811ba9d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), Democrats currently hold a significant nine point advantage on the congressional ballot. Those numbers should encourage Democrats. They should also be a warning.
A record 45 percent of Americans identified as independents in 2025, according to[ Gallup](https://substack.com/redirect/05af9112-0bc7-4874-9016-1ce9eb52330f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), while just 27 percent called themselves Democrats and the same share called themselves Republicans. Independents are the fastest growing political party in the country. These are also voters who move the needle:[ independents favored Joe Biden in 2020](https://substack.com/redirect/c2e1c38e-e5d1-486d-ac85-dafafba65cee?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) by 9 points but[ split evenly between Kamala Harris and Donald Trump](https://substack.com/redirect/901c9e79-c021-4517-929c-118656899e78?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) four years later. If American politicians want their votes, they have to earn them.
That was certainly true in Bucks County in 2006. More than 2,000 volunteers knocked on roughly 160,000 doors for our campaign. We competed in Republican communities because there was simply no other way to win. Many of the voters I needed had supported George W. Bush. Some had voted for him twice. In purple Bucks County,
My job was not to lecture those voters about why they had been wrong to support Bush. It was to understand why they had voted the way they did, tell them what I believed and give them a reason to make a different choice. Yes, I was making the case for why the incumbent should be fired. But I also had to make the case for why I should be hired. That sounds obvious, but increasingly, it is not. Much of modern politics, particularly online, is organized around affirmation rather than persuasion. Too often, it has become a form of political infotainment. Candidates are rewarded for proving that they understand the language, priorities and enemies of their own faction to gin up their base for donations and support. The electorate in a Democratic or Republican primary is not the electorate candidates will face in November. In districts like Bucks County, [independents are more than 18% of the electorate](https://substack.com/redirect/fc702fae-be01-4ed7-8420-3b9c462006c2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), with Democrats composing 40% and Republicans 42%, so the general election requires a much broader appeal, especially after Donald Trump edged out Joe Biden here two years ago.
This does not mean Democrats should become ideologically uniform or sprint toward the center on every issue once they win next Tuesday. This is especially true in purple counties and states like Pennsylvania -- we are one of only three states with US senators from different parties and a divided state government. Pluralism, even within one's own party, does not require everybody to believe the same thing. It requires something more basic: respect for people who disagree with you. Millions of Americans voted for Donald Trump because they believed he would improve their lives. Many are now disappointed. Democrats should simply ask whether the president they supported has delivered and explain what they would do differently. Those voters need somewhere else to go.
A voter should not have to apologize for his 2024 ballot before he is welcomed into a Democratic coalition in 2026. Give people a reason to change their minds without demanding that they first confess they were bad people for having held them. Respecting Republican voters is not the same as excusing Republican leaders, and Democrats should criticize the president forcefully where they believe he has failed.
That was one of the great lessons of 2006. The national environment opened the door for Democrats, but voters still had to walk through it. In purple Bucks County, enough Republicans and independents decided that they could disagree with me about some things and still trust me to represent them.
The political climate is once again moving in Democrats' direction. But politics can be fickle, and favorable conditions alone do not win elections. People do.
Some on the political right are discrediting polling even though the writing is on the wall as Congress has deferred to the executive branch, while many on the left don't accept the fact that while we're heading toward another change election, it's not necessarily because Americans want dramatic policy changes. The last six federal elections have all resulted in a change of party control in the House, Senate, or the White House, and next week - November 3rd -- will make it seven change elections in a row. And while most Americans want change, it better be the kind that responsibly ends the unnecessary war in Iran and makes the cost of living much more affordable, both at the pump and at home.
**Since 1877, All Seven Twice-Elected Presidents Who Finished their Terms Ended Facing an Opposition Senate**

graphic via Bruce Mehlman's Six Chart Sunday newsletter.
Whatever happens next Tuesday, let's hope we use this as an opportunity to remember God gave us each two ears, two eyes, but only one mouth for a reason - to harness the skill to truly listen and respect viewpoints that aren't necessarily our own.
The people whose minds differ from Democrats or Republicans are not their enemies. They are our fellow Americans. We should respect them enough to ask for their votes and to give them a reason to believe in political public service again.
